newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian MPs mention the unmentionable tax.
newsitem.headline: Australian MPs mention the unmentionable tax.

text.p: Australia's political leaders are mentioning the unmentionable: the possibility of a value-added consumption tax.

Riding high in opinion polls, members of the ruling Liberal-National coalition are publicly discussing the merits of a goods and services tax (GST) -- a proposal regarded as political poison since it cost them a supposedly unloseable general election in 1993.

"I think the party does want to move into a consumption tax or a GST, but the coalition and the leadership of the coalition are very nervous about it," said Ron Boswell, Senate leader for the junior coalition partner, the National Party.
"I think the National Party will want it on the agenda for the second term, but we don't want to frighten the horses," he said on television on Sunday.
Ministers invariably reject the suggestion -- for now.
"There won't be a GST in this (term of) parliament," Prime Minister John Howard said in response to Boswell.
"You ask me about the next parliament when we are coming towards it."
But Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer acknowledged that the debate was on again.
"Clearly there is going to be further consideration of tax matters but that is down the track," he said, adding that the GST was not on the agenda.
Economists say a GST would encourage saving, by discouraging consumption, and help beat tax avoiders, who would have to pay at least something when they spend their money.

Although Australia has some of the highest tax rates in the developed world -- middle class employees can pay marginal tax rates of almost 50 percent -- tax revenues as a proportion of national income are actually among the lowest.

In 1993 the conservatives wanted to abolish all indirect taxes and replace them with a comprehensive GST levied at 15 percent at each stage of production and producing a net gain in revenue. Income taxes, accordingly, would have fallen.

But the conservative coalition emphatically dropped the GST after the 1993 election, in which then prime minister Paul Keating told voters it would be a harmful and unnecessary imposition. Keating won, despite 11 percent unemployment.
Desperate to end 13 years of Labor rule, the coalition entered the 1996 election with an absolute promise that there would be no GST in its first term in government.
Their subsequent landslide victory -- amid much more benign economic conditions than in 1993 -- only reinforced impressions that the GST was wholly responsible for the conservatives' previous rout.

But their voter support has risen even further since the election -- the coalition is now almost twice as far ahead as it was in March -- and conservative politicians have been increasingly willing to raise the possibility.
The Liberal state premier of Victoria, Jeff Kennett, has been publicly pushing for tax reform since soon after the March election.
At first he was shouted down by his conservative colleagues. Now, he attracts only the sort of "not just yet" response that Howard gave on Sunday.
